name: Minecraft
tagline: Voxel sandbox game with survival and creative modes, multiplayer servers, and a two-decade mod ecosystem.

pricing.basis: one-time purchase per account, Realms subscription sold separately
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A coding agent can absolutely give you a voxel world: chunked terrain, block placing and breaking, a first person controller, maybe some crude crafting. What it cannot give you is the thing people actually bought, which is fifteen years of content design, mob behaviour, redstone logic, biome generation tuned by thousands of hours of playtesting, and the server your friends are already on. Minecraft is also not a workflow you are paying monthly to avoid; it is a one-time purchase in the price range of two sandwiches. The mod and server ecosystem is the real product and it is welded to the official clients and protocol. Build the voxel engine because it is genuinely fun to build, not because it replaces anything.
coreLoopDIY: A browser voxel sandbox where you fly around procedurally generated terrain and place or break blocks, saved locally.
requirements: Node 20 and a modern browser with WebGL2
block textures you draw or license yourself, the originals are not yours to ship
patience for chunk meshing performance work
whatYouLose: Every friend and public server, since you cannot speak the official protocol without reimplementing it
The mod, plugin, datapack and resource pack ecosystem, which is most of the long-tail value
Survival game design: mobs, hunger, combat balance, enchanting, the nether, progression that actually hooks
Twenty years of world generation tuning, so your terrain will look like noise with grass on top
Cross-platform clients, console parity, and anything your kid can actually play on a tablet
moatNotes: The engine is the easy part. The IP, the mob design, and the fact that everyone's friends are already inside are the hard parts.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because it is one payment for a game that has had continuous design work since 2009, and because the people they want to play with are in it. Nobody is paying Minecraft to automate a chore; they are paying for a place. A self-built voxel engine is a tech demo you show someone for ninety seconds, which is a completely different product from a world you spend four hundred hours in.
notes: The voxel engine is a weekend; the game is not. The moat is content rights plus every friend already having an account and a server.
prompt:
Build a browser based voxel sandbox toy in an empty folder. One stack, no options.

Stack: TypeScript, Vite, Three.js. No React. No backend. No accounts, no telemetry, no network calls at all.

What to build:
- A fixed size world of 16x16 chunks, each chunk 16 wide, 16 deep, 64 tall, stored as a flat Uint8Array of block ids.
- Terrain generation from 2D simplex noise for height plus a second noise channel for a dirt/stone/sand split. Seed is a constant in src/config.ts.
- Greedy or at minimum per-face culled chunk meshing: never emit faces between two solid blocks. Rebuild only the dirty chunk on edit.
- Block ids: air, grass, dirt, stone, sand, wood, leaves, glass. One texture atlas PNG that you generate yourself at build time with a small script drawing flat colored squares with noise. Do not download or reference any real game textures.
- First person controls: WASD, mouse look via pointer lock, space to jump, shift to sprint, F to toggle fly mode. Simple AABB collision against the voxel grid, gravity, step up of 0.5 blocks.
- Raycast from the camera up to 6 blocks: left click breaks, right click places the selected block. Highlight the targeted face with a wireframe box.
- Hotbar of the 7 placeable blocks, keys 1-7, rendered as plain DOM overlay.
- Save and load the whole world to IndexedDB on a 5 second debounce and on page hide. One world slot. A button to regenerate from scratch with confirm.

Explicitly out of scope: multiplayer, mobs, crafting, inventory beyond the hotbar, day/night cycle, water simulation, lighting beyond a single directional light plus ambient, infinite worlds.

Deliverables: npm run dev works, npm run build produces a static dist that opens from a file server. README with controls and a one paragraph note on where the chunk meshing will fall over if the world gets bigger. No .env needed since there are no secrets.
